title_candidates: Claude Code built a game from two pictures — then caught its own mobile bug
summary: Simon Willison turned two old game-concept images into a playable browser game with Claude Code, GitHub Pages, frequent previews, and automated mobile tests.

primary_source.title: One-shotting a Raccoon Heist game using Claude Fable 5
primary_source.author: Simon Willison
key_facts: Simon Willison gave Claude Fable 5 two images from a 2022 game concept and asked it to turn the idea into a complete browser game.
He ran the experiment from his phone in Claude Code for web, asking for mobile support, frequent GitHub commits, a running notes file, and independent decision-making.
Willison used GitHub Pages to preview the agent's branch after each push rather than waiting until the project was finished.
Claude chose Three.js, generated textures through a separate image API, and used Playwright to inspect desktop and mobile layouts.
The testing pass found that the raccoon was invisible at mobile widths, after which Claude corrected the layout.
Claude reported seven commits and automated playthroughs across desktop, portrait-phone, and landscape-phone viewports.
Willison found the result technically impressive and mobile-friendly but too easy and repetitive to count as a good finished game.
He recommends small game projects as a fun, relatively low-risk way to learn what agents can and cannot do.

supporting_sources.title: Use Claude Code on the web
key_facts: Anthropic documents that web sessions clone GitHub repositories, run work in isolated cloud environments, and push changes to branches for review.
The web workflow preserves the session and code changes so users can inspect what happened before merging.

supporting_sources.title: Quickstart for GitHub Pages
key_facts: GitHub Pages can publish a static site from a selected repository branch and folder.
GitHub warns that publishing can take up to ten minutes after the Pages settings are saved.

prerequisites: A Claude Pro, Max, Team, or eligible Enterprise account with Claude Code on the web
Permission to publish the result publicly; use only simple shapes or non-sensitive images you own

steps.instruction: On GitHub, choose New repository, create a public repository named raccoon-mini, turn Add README on, and click Create repository. Stop if the idea, repository name, or any asset must remain private.
Open Claude Code on the web, connect GitHub if prompted, select raccoon-mini and its main branch, then choose Plan mode so Claude shows its approach before editing.

Ask for a one-screen, mobile-friendly catching game in one index.html using only HTML, CSS, JavaScript, emoji, or CSS shapes. Require Start and Restart buttons, keyboard and touch controls, a score, a 30-second timer, and tests. Forbid packages, APIs, tracking, uploads, network requests, secrets, and private or copyrighted images. Approve only if the plan keeps those limits.

When Claude finishes, inspect Files changed before merging. Continue only if the changes are limited to the small game and documentation; stop if you see credentials, personal data, external URLs, analytics, Actions, or unfamiliar generated files.
Merge the reviewed pull request. Open Settings, then Pages; choose Deploy from a branch, select main and /(root), and save.

Open the Pages URL on both a phone and a desktop. Verify Start, movement, scoring, the 30-second ending, and Restart yourself. If any check fails, disable Pages or stop sharing the link until it is fixed.

risk_flags: Signal already covered the Fable 5 release; keep this article focused on the build-preview-test workflow rather than model specifications.
The source experiment gave the agent an external image API key; Signal's guide deliberately uses simple local assets and forbids secrets, packages, and network requests.
GitHub Pages is public in this guide. Readers must stop if the idea, repository name, or assets should remain private.
The source author found the one-shot result repetitive and not good as a finished game; do not present one-shot generation as production-ready.
The 20-minute guide creates a smaller one-file game instead of attempting to reproduce the source's 3D project.
